PierreJanineh_TechDebtMCP_135-16a54f0f.message: The user-supplied `path` parameter is passed directly to `fileExists`, `getFileStats`, and `readFile` without validating via `path.isAbsolute()` or normalizing via `path.resolve()`. A malicious client can supply a relative traversal string like `../../../../etc/passwd` to read arbitrary files, bypassing the intent of the size guard entirely. The project's AGENTS.md explicitly mandates these checks before any filesystem operation (Issues #125, #126) and no such validation is present anywhere in the server directory.

ALLOWED_FLAGS_RE = /^[gimsuy]*$/ excludes the `d` flag (hasIndices), which is a valid ECMAScript 2022 flag supported since Node.js 16. The project declares `engines.node >= 18`, making `d` a fully valid flag on every supported runtime. Any user passing `flags: 'd'` to `add_custom_rule` or `validate_custom_pattern` gets an incorrect 'Invalid regex flags' rejection, and the flag is silently stripped at execution time, changing matching behavior without warning.

The production `CustomRulesEngine` is instantiated without an `onRuleError` callback. When the defense-in-depth guard in `executePattern` fires at runtime (e.g., an oversized or invalid pattern loaded from `.techdebtrc.json` bypassing `validatePattern`), the branch `if (this.onRuleError)` is false and the error is silently discarded. The MCP client receives an empty issues array for those rules with no indication that they were skipped, making the tool silently unreliable for config-loaded rules.

ALLOWED_FLAGS_RE = /^[gimsuy]*$/ uses `*` (zero or more), so it accepts duplicate flag characters such as `'gg'`. Passing `'gg'` directly to `new RegExp()` throws a SyntaxError; the deduplication inside both `validatePattern` and `executePattern` silently masks this. The stated contract of `validatePattern` is that a passing result means the pattern is ready to use, but a caller who constructs `new RegExp(pattern.pattern, pattern.flags)` from a 'valid' result with duplicate flags will get a thrown exception. The regex should enforce uniqueness, e.g. `/^[gimsuy]{0,6}$/` with a uniqueness check.

When `pattern.flags` contains disallowed characters, `validatePattern` pushes a flags-error and then continues to compile the regex using normalized (stripped) flags. This means a pattern that is syntactically invalid only when combined with its declared flags (rare but possible with flag-specific syntax like `\p{}` requiring `u`) will be compiled with `u` stripped and may not surface an 'Invalid regex pattern' error. The two validation concerns — flags and pattern — are tested independently rather than together, so the reported validity does not reflect the actual behavior at execution time when both flags and pattern interact.

The two new error messages `File not found: ${path}` and `Could not read file stats for: ${path}` embed the raw `path` value, which is typically an absolute filesystem path, in the MCP error response. The project's AGENTS.md security section states 'Use getRelativePath() in error messages returned to clients — never leak absolute filesystem paths' (Issue #129). These are new error paths introduced by this PR that do not follow that convention.

The regex flag normalization logic (stripping invalid characters and deduplication) is duplicated between `validatePattern` (lines 235-242) and `executePattern` (lines 119-123). This logic should be extracted into a private helper function to avoid code duplication and ensure that validation and execution always use the identical flag processing rules.

The code handles a null return from `getFileStats` by throwing an `McpError`, but there is no corresponding test case to verify this error path. The new tests in `src/server/__tests__/handlers.test.ts` only cover the file size limit being exceeded and met, but not the case where file stats cannot be retrieved.

This changelog overstates the security fix: limiting pattern length and flags does not prevent catastrophic-backtracking ReDoS for short patterns that are still executed synchronously. Please either implement an actual ReDoS mitigation before claiming prevention or reword this entry to accurately describe the narrower guards added.

simnaut_emdash_2-41d75006.message: The AT Protocol login route uses `url.origin` (the raw internal request origin) as `baseUrl` for the OAuth client, rather than `getPublicOrigin(url, emdash?.config)`. Behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy, the internal origin is `http://localhost:4321` while the browser-facing origin is `https://example.com`. The AT Protocol PDS will attempt to fetch the client metadata document from the internal URL (unreachable), and the `client_id` will be wrong, causing the OAuth authorization flow to fail in all production reverse-proxy deployments. GitHub/Google OAuth in `[provider].ts` correctly use `getPublicOrigin(url, emdash?.config)`. The same problem exists in `callback.ts` line 42 and `setup-admin.ts` line 56.

Same reverse-proxy bug as in login.ts: `baseUrl` is set to `url.origin` instead of `getPublicOrigin(url, emdash?.config)`. The callback route creates an OAuthClient with the internal URL, which must match the `client_id` and `redirect_uri` registered during authorization. While both authorize and callback using the same wrong URL means they're consistent with each other, the `client_id` still points to an unreachable metadata URL in production, breaking the OAuth flow.

The `CREATE INDEX` statement for `idx_{table}_deleted_published_id` is missing `IF NOT EXISTS`. The `SchemaRegistry.createCollectionTable()` (also changed in this PR, at registry.ts line 600) creates the same index when any new collection is created. If a user runs the version of EmDash that adds the SchemaRegistry index creation (part of this PR) and creates a new collection, then for some reason runs migrations again (e.g., a test environment that tears down and rebuilds), migration 034 would fail with 'index already exists'. This is the exact issue that was documented as fixed in migration 033 (`CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`).

Same reverse-proxy bug: `baseUrl = url.origin` instead of `getPublicOrigin()`. During the setup wizard, if the server is behind a reverse proxy, the AT Protocol OAuth URL generated here will use the internal origin as `client_id`, causing the PDS to fail when it attempts to fetch the metadata document or validate the redirect URI.

The fast-path for plugin routes outside `/_emdash/` (e.g., `/.well-known/atproto-client-metadata.json`) bypasses the entire middleware chain, including CSRF protection. While GET requests don't need CSRF protection, any future state-changing route injected by an auth provider at a non-`/_emdash/` path would receive no CSRF check. The fast-path calls `next()` directly without invoking `checkPublicCsrf`. This is currently OK because `client-metadata.json` is GET-only, but the architecture silently skips CSRF for all methods on fast-path routes.

The `/auth/mode` endpoint is public and returns the configured auth provider list (`providers`). When `emdash` is not initialized (e.g., before first setup), `emdash?.config?.authProviders` is `undefined` and `providers` defaults to `[]`. However, `getAuthMode(emdash?.config)` is called with `undefined` config, which returns the default passkey mode. This is correct. But `emdash?.db` check for signup detection is done with optional chaining, so when the DB is uninitialized, `signupEnabled` stays `false`. The catch block silently swallows errors from the `allowed_domains` query. If the table query fails for reasons other than the table not existing (e.g., DB corruption), the signup state would incorrectly report false. This is minor but could mask real DB errors.

konturio_disaster-ninja-fe_1230-d169e9da.message: layer('disable') and layer('enable') are not valid reatom v2 API calls. LayerAtom is AtomSelfBinded<LogicalLayerState, LogicalLayerActions>; actions must be dispatched via store.dispatch([layer.disable()]) and store.dispatch([layer.enable()]), as demonstrated in applyNewLayerSource.ts. Calling the atom as a plain function with a string argument invokes the reducer directly with an invalid argument — not the action handler — so the remounting logic is a no-op. store is not imported in GenericRenderer.ts, so this cannot be fixed without adding that import.

layersOrderManager.init() is called without first calling layersOrderManager.destroy(). The init() method unconditionally pushes a new layersSettingsAtom subscription to the private _unsubscribe array (layersOrder.ts line 51-54). Every basemap switch therefore leaks one subscription. Additionally, destroy() never clears _unsubscribe, so previously-cancelled functions accumulate across successive init/destroy cycles.

styledata is the wrong event to wait for after setStyle. MapLibre fires styledata for each incremental style update and it can fire before the basemap's own layers are fully parsed. As a result, map.getStyle().layers may be incomplete when layersOrderManager.init() reads it to set _baseMapFirstLayerIdx, producing an incorrect index that causes subsequent user layers to be inserted below basemap layers. The correct event to await full style load after setStyle is style.load.

There is no guard against concurrent style switches. If willMount or willSourceUpdate is called again (e.g. rapid toggling) while the previous setStyle has not yet fired its styledata event, a second map.once('styledata', ...) listener is queued. Each styledata event will then trigger the next queued handler, causing double init of layersOrderManager and double remount of all layers, leaving the map in an unpredictable state.

mapLibreParentsIds.clear() removes all maplibre-layer-to-UI-layer mappings immediately, including entries for layers that will not be successfully remounted (because the remounting API is broken). Any concurrent call to layersOrderManager that still references those IDs (e.g. _getMountedOrderedLayers) will silently skip those layers with a 'id was not found' warning and produce wrong ordering decisions.

The test validates the broken layer('disable') / layer('enable') call pattern by mocking otherLayer as a plain vi.fn() and checking call[0] === 'disable'. Real LayerAtom instances cannot be invoked this way; the production code path is broken, but the test passes because the mock accepts any arguments. This gives false confidence that remounting works.

After setStyle is called, all previously added sources and layers are wiped from the map. The basemap renderer itself never adds anything to this._layerIds for the maplibre-style-url branch, so _removeLayers is a no-op on unmount. However, willUnMount will still attempt to remove this._sourceId (SOURCE_IN_AREA_PREFIX + id) from the map even though it was never added, producing a console.warn on every basemap layer unmount.

layersToRemount is captured by reading mountedLayersAtom.getState() before setStyle. If the atom state has diverged from the last-updated snapshot (the file documents a known reatom v2 bug where atom state can be stale and the workaround _lastUpdatedState_DO_NOT_USE_OR_YOU_WILL_BE_FIRED exists), some mounted layers will be silently missed and not remounted after the style change.

After `map.setStyle(styleUrl)`, execution falls through to the rest of `_updateMap` (the `if (!isVisible) this.willHide(...)`, tooltip provider registration, click listener registration, etc., starting at line 247). For a basemap layer this state is mostly empty, but it does mean `willHide` may be invoked while the new style is still loading asynchronously, and the layer-list cleanup runs before the styledata callback fires. Consider `return`ing after scheduling the styledata handler so the basemap branch doesn't accidentally execute logic intended only for data layers.

This remounts the snapshot taken before the async style change completed. If a user disables one of these layers while the new style is loading, this handler still calls `enable` on that stale layer and turns it back on, overriding the user's latest choice. Check the current mounted/enabled state when the style event fires instead of unconditionally disabling and enabling the snapshot.

The remount snapshot includes any previously mounted basemap because it only filters out the newly selected layer. Base layers are mutually exclusive (`src/core/logical_layers/constants.ts:14-17`), but during a switch the old basemap can still be in `mountedLayersAtom`; the later `disable`/`enable` remount sequence will re-enable that old basemap and can switch the style back. Filter remounts to non-basemap overlay layers or use the current enabled set after mutual exclusion has settled.

The test name and assertion message say layers are remounted, but this only verifies the `disable` call. If the production code failed to call `enable` afterward, the test would still pass while overlays remain unmounted after a basemap switch. Assert both calls, preferably in order, so the remount behavior is actually covered.

This setup only includes a generic mounted layer, so it misses the failure mode where another `maplibre-style-url` basemap is still mounted during the switch. Because the `base` category is mutually exclusive (`src/core/logical_layers/constants.ts:14-17`), coverage should include an existing basemap in `mountedLayersAtom` to ensure the remount logic does not re-enable the old style layer.

cmik_apilix_12-0c34439a.message: bcryptjs and jsonwebtoken are recorded in the lockfile's root-package dependencies section but are absent from server/package.json. The PR description says these were added to fix 'Cannot find module' crashes, but the package.json diff only adds simple-git. A fresh `npm install` in the server directory will not install bcryptjs or jsonwebtoken, and `npm ci` will fail with a lockfile/manifest mismatch.

The `dataDir` value used to construct repo paths in all three git sync routes is taken directly from the request body (`req.body.dataDir`). Any caller can supply an arbitrary `dataDir` (e.g. `/`) to make the server create git repositories and write workspace files anywhere on the filesystem that the server process can access. The path-traversal check on `workspaceId` does nothing to constrain `dataDir` itself. The routes should reject any client-supplied `dataDir` and use only `process.env.APILIX_DATA_DIR`.

The path-traversal guard `repoDir.startsWith(path.resolve(repoBase))` is missing a trailing path separator. If `repoBase` is `/data/git-sync/workspaces`, a `workspaceId` of `../workspaces_evil/x` resolves to `/data/git-sync/workspaces_evil/x`, which starts with `/data/git-sync/workspaces` and passes the check. The same bug exists at lines 1083 and 1118. The fix, consistent with `assertInsideUserData` in electron/main.js, is to append `path.sep` to the base when comparing.

`syncConfig.lastSynced` is never written by `writeSyncConfig` in storageDriver.ts, and the `SyncConfig` objects constructed in WorkspaceManagerModal never include a `lastSynced` field. As a result `localTs` is always `null`, the condition `remoteTs && localTs && remoteTs > localTs` is always false, and conflict detection is completely disabled — every pull silently overwrites local changes without warning.

Conflict detection compares timestamps as strings (`remoteTs > localTs`). The HTTP adapter returns `Last-Modified` (RFC 2822 format, e.g. `Mon, 01 Jan 2024 00:00:00 GMT`) and S3 also returns `Last-Modified` in RFC 2822. RFC 2822 strings are not lexicographically sortable, so the comparison produces incorrect results for those providers. All timestamps should be parsed into `Date` objects before comparing.

`saveTimer` is stored in React `useState` rather than `useRef`. Every time the 300ms debounce timer is set, `setSaveTimer(t)` triggers an additional component re-render. Because `saveTimer` is not in the effect dependency array, the effect closure captures a stale value of it, making the `if (saveTimer) clearTimeout(saveTimer)` guard unreliable. The cleanup function (`return () => clearTimeout(t)`) already handles timer cancellation correctly; `saveTimer` state serves no purpose and adds unnecessary renders. Use `useRef` instead.

When the user switches workspaces, the dependency-change triggers the save effect to re-run, which first runs the cleanup (`clearTimeout(t)`) cancelling any pending 300ms debounce timer for the previous workspace before it fires. Edits made to workspace A in the 300ms window before switching are silently lost because the save for workspace A is cancelled and a new timer starts for workspace B. There is no flush-before-switch logic in either handleSwitch implementation.

In `writeSyncConfig`, if the Electron API's `readJsonFile` call throws (e.g. corrupted file, permission error), the `catch` silently falls through with `store` still set to `{}`. The subsequent `lsWrite` then writes only the current workspace's config, erasing all other workspaces' sync credentials from localStorage. To fix: read the existing localStorage store as the fallback when the file read fails, rather than using the empty `store`.

The IPC handlers for `read-json-file`, `write-json-file`, `delete-file`, and `list-dir` use synchronous Node.js filesystem APIs (`fs.readFileSync`, `fs.writeFileSync`, `fs.mkdirSync`, `fs.readdirSync`, `fs.unlinkSync`) directly on the Electron main process thread. These block the main process event loop for the duration of each I/O operation. On slow disks or with large workspace files, this can freeze the entire Electron window. All handlers should use `fs.promises` equivalents.

`handleDelete` dispatches `DELETE_WORKSPACE` and conditionally `SWITCH_WORKSPACE` (updating in-memory state immediately) and then calls `StorageDriver.writeManifest`. If `writeManifest` fails, the on-disk manifest still contains the deleted workspace but the in-memory state does not. On next app restart the deleted workspace will reappear in the manifest but its data file has already been deleted by `deleteWorkspace`, resulting in an empty workspace silently presented to the user. Errors from `writeManifest` are not caught or surfaced.

The S3 adapter relies on `window.electronAPI.getPresignedUrl` to function. If this API is not available (e.g., when running in a browser), it throws an error. However, the UI in `WorkspaceManagerModal.tsx` does not disable the S3 sync option for non-Electron environments, leading to a poor user experience where the user can configure S3 sync only to have it fail at runtime.

`simple-git` is an optional dependency. If it fails to load, the server continues to run. However, the error is caught and `simpleGit` remains `undefined`. The health check endpoint `/health` will still return a 200 OK status, which could mislead monitoring systems into thinking the service is fully functional when a core feature (git sync) is unavailable.

`bcryptjs` and `jsonwebtoken` are added to `package-lock.json` but not declared in `server/package.json`. With npm's lockfile v3, packages listed at the top level of `node_modules/...` without a matching root dependency entry are treated as extraneous and will be pruned by `npm ci` / `npm install`. Either declare these in `package.json` (as the PR description implied) or remove their entries from the lockfile to keep both files consistent.

`s3Adapter` calls `(window as any).electronAPI.getPresignedUrl(...)`, but no `getPresignedUrl` is exposed in `electron/preload.js` and no `get-presigned-url` IPC handler is registered in `electron/main.js`. As a result, every push/pull/timestamp call for the S3 provider will throw `S3 presigned URL generation requires Electron (not available in browser mode)` even when running inside Electron. The S3 provider is documented as a supported, Electron-only option (see `WORKSPACES.md` §7 and `README.md`), but it is non-functional in this PR. Either implement the `get-presigned-url` IPC channel (and add `getPresignedUrl` to preload) or remove S3 from the provider list and documentation until it lands.

The history index is sliced to `MAX_SNAPSHOTS` (50), but the corresponding snapshot files written to `userData/workspaces/{workspaceId}/snapshots/{snapshotId}.json` are never deleted from disk when their entry is evicted from the index. Because a new snapshot is created on every debounced save (every ~300ms of user idle time after a change), this leaks disk space indefinitely and orphans potentially large workspace JSON blobs that no UI can ever surface. Before slicing the updated index, capture the dropped entries and call `StorageDriver.deleteFile` (or a new `deleteSnapshot` helper) for each evicted `snapshotId`.

A snapshot is created on **every** debounced workspace save, which fires roughly every time any field changes (collections, environments, variables, cookies, mock state, even the active workspace id). With `MAX_SNAPSHOTS = 50` and a 300 ms debounce, the rolling history window covers only ~15 seconds of editing in practice, making the History tab almost useless for actual rollback. Consider gating snapshot creation behind a longer minimum interval (e.g. only one snapshot per N minutes, or only when a structural change is detected by `diffSnapshots`).

The feature comparison table marks Git as **not requiring Electron** (`✗`), but `gitAdapter.ts` calls `getDataDir()` from `storageDriver`, which returns `null` in browser mode, and then sends `dataDir: null` to the server. The server route at `/api/sync/git/push` (and pull/timestamp) explicitly requires `dataDir`: `if (!workspaceId || !data || !config?.remote || !dataDir) return res.status(400)...`. So in practice, Git sync also requires Electron unless `APILIX_DATA_DIR` is set in the server's environment. Either clarify this row (e.g. "Requires Electron or `APILIX_DATA_DIR` on server") or update the adapter/server to be browser-friendly.

In `handleDelete`, `state.activeWorkspaceId` is read both before and after `dispatch({ type: 'DELETE_WORKSPACE', ... })`, but the closure's `state.activeWorkspaceId` does not update synchronously. The subsequent `await StorageDriver.writeManifest(...)` therefore persists `activeWorkspaceId: state.activeWorkspaceId === id ? fallback.id : state.activeWorkspaceId` using the *pre-dispatch* value — which still works for the current case, but the logic is fragile and easy to break. More importantly, the debounced save effect in `store.tsx` will fire a moment later and overwrite this manifest write with the new state anyway, so this explicit `writeManifest` call is redundant and the two writes can race on slow disks. Consider removing the explicit `writeManifest` here and relying on the debounced effect, or routing all manifest writes through a single helper.

`TeamTab` imports `dispatch` from `useApp()` but never uses it; it also reads `activeWorkspace.teamServerUrl` and writes to local `serverUrl` state but never persists the entered Server URL or JWT token anywhere (no `StorageDriver.writeSyncConfig` call). After "Test connection" succeeds the credentials are simply discarded on tab change or modal close, contradicting `WORKSPACES.md` §9 step 6 which says clicking "Test connection in the Team tab" is part of the connect-and-sync flow. Either remove the unused `dispatch`, wire up the team-server credential save, or document that this tab is informational only.

The S3 adapter calls `electronAPI.getPresignedUrl`, but the preload bridge and Electron main process do not expose or handle any `getPresignedUrl` IPC method. As a result, every S3 push/pull/timestamp operation will throw before reaching S3.

These S3 field keys do not match what the S3 adapter reads: the UI stores `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`, while `s3Adapter` sends `config.keyId` and `config.secret` to the presigner. Even after adding the missing IPC handler, S3 requests would be generated with undefined credentials.

Despite the encryption helper below and the type/docs saying credentials are encrypted, this writes provider config directly to `sync-config.json` and localStorage. Tokens and access keys entered in the Sync tab are therefore persisted in plaintext in Electron mode.

Switching workspaces reads the target workspace and dispatches immediately without flushing the active workspace. Since `AppProvider` persists on a 300 ms debounce and cancels the pending timer on state changes, edits made shortly before switching can be dropped instead of saved to the previous workspace.

This workspace switch path also bypasses a flush of the currently active workspace before replacing state. With the debounced persistence in `AppProvider`, recent edits can be lost when switching from the manager modal before the pending save fires.

This only removes old entries from the history index; the snapshot files that were sliced off remain on disk. The documented 50-snapshot cap will not cap disk usage, and auto-save can keep accumulating orphaned `snapshots/*.json` files indefinitely.

These mutating git sync endpoints are exposed on the same unauthenticated Express app with global `cors()` enabled (server/index.js:43). A malicious web page can issue requests to the user's local server and cause git commits/pushes using supplied remotes/credentials; add an app-local authorization/CSRF guard before exposing filesystem and network side effects.

When the user resolves a conflict with `Keep Local`, `syncPull` returns `null`, but this branch reports “Remote is empty — nothing to pull”. That gives the wrong result message for a conflict resolution and may lead users to believe the remote has no data.

Push reads the workspace from StorageDriver instead of the current in-memory state. Because workspace persistence is debounced, clicking Push immediately after edits can upload the previous on-disk version and omit the user's latest changes.

Duplicating a workspace reads the source data from StorageDriver. For the active workspace, recent in-memory edits may not have reached disk yet because saves are debounced, so the duplicate can be created without the latest changes.

Creating a new workspace switches `activeWorkspaceId` without first persisting the current workspace. With the debounced save in `AppProvider`, any edits made shortly before creating the workspace can be discarded when the pending save is cancelled.

`URL.username` and `URL.password` setters perform their own percent-encoding, so passing `encodeURIComponent(...)` here double-encodes credentials that contain reserved characters such as `%`, `@`, or `:`. Those tokens/passwords will fail authentication when pushed.

`URL.username`/`password` already encode assigned values. Encoding before assignment double-encodes credentials with reserved characters, causing authenticated pulls to fail for valid tokens/passwords containing those characters.

`URL.username`/`password` already encode assigned values. Encoding before assignment double-encodes credentials with reserved characters, so timestamp fetches can fail authentication for valid credentials.

Deleting a workspace only removes `{id}.json`; its `workspaces/{id}/history.json` and `workspaces/{id}/snapshots/*` directory are left behind. Deleted workspace data can remain on disk indefinitely through snapshots.

Workspace deletion removes the workspace JSON and manifest entry, but it never removes the workspace's entry from `sync-config.json`. Any tokens/access keys saved for the deleted workspace remain on disk after deletion.

The PR description says this change only declares missing `jsonwebtoken` and `bcryptjs` dependencies, but this file introduces extensive workspace/sync documentation for a much larger feature set. The description should be updated so reviewers and release notes reflect the actual scope and risk of the PR.

It directly invokes the mocked `chat_interface.send_request_to_open_ai` and then asserts against the return value the mock was configured to produce. DisciplinedSoftware_Codebase-Conversion_.message: The .env loader in convert.py does not strip surrounding quotes from values. If a user writes `LLM_API_KEY="ghp_abc"` in .env, the stored value will be `"ghp_abc"` (with quotes) because only `_val.strip()` is called, not quote-stripping. The llm_client.py loader (also used at LLMClient init time) does strip quotes, but since convert.py's loader runs first and uses `os.environ.setdefault`, the already-set (quoted) value is never overridden. The result is that the API key sent in the Authorization header will include literal quote characters, causing silent authentication failure.

`_try_download_file` does not clean up a partially-downloaded file on failure. `urlretrieve` writes data as it arrives; if the connection drops after more than 100 bytes, `dest.stat().st_size > 100` returns True and the function returns True with a corrupt or truncated file. If the download delivers ≤100 bytes before failing, the partial file remains on disk and `dest.exists()` is True. On any subsequent run the file is found in the cache and `missing` will not include it, so the corrupt file is silently used instead of being re-fetched.

`_try_download_tarball` calls `output_dir.rglob('*.f')` to copy extracted files into the cache dir, but the cache dir (`output_dir/fortran/blas/`) is itself inside `output_dir`. Any files already cached there will be found by `rglob` and `shutil.copy2(extracted, cache / extracted.name)` will attempt to copy a file to itself, raising `shutil.SameFileError`. brexhq_CrabTrap_15-5ef0884c.message: The `query` method (called by both `QuerySummaries` and `Query`) creates its own `context.Background()` and ignores the request context passed by callers. `Count` correctly accepts and uses a `context.Context` parameter, so HTTP request cancellation and deadlines apply to it. But `QuerySummaries` runs outside any deadline: if a client disconnects mid-flight, the database query continues until completion, holding a pgxpool connection. Under load, this can exhaust the connection pool.

`Count` and `QuerySummaries` execute as two independent, non-transactional queries. Any row inserted between the two calls means `total` is understated relative to what `QuerySummaries` sees, causing `has_more` to read `false` on a page that is actually the last full page (one page boundary will appear to have no continuation). Conversely, rows deleted between the calls (e.g., by a retention job) make `total` overstated, so `has_more` stays `true` after the real last page, causing the client to request an empty next page. Wrapping both in a repeatable-read transaction or using a single query with a window function (`COUNT(*) OVER ()`) would fix this.

When `QuerySummaries` fails (i.e., the pgx `Query` call returns an error), `query` returns `nil`. The handler converts `nil` to `[]types.AuditEntry{}` and responds HTTP 200 with `{"entries":[], "total": N, "has_more": true}` — an empty entry list paired with a positive total and `has_more: true`. The UI will show zero rows but keep the "Load more" button active, looping forever. The nil return from `query` signals a DB error and should be converted to a 500 response, the same way a `Count` error already is.

`toggleExpanded` calls `setExpandedId(rowId)` unconditionally, then checks `if (!entry.id || ...)` and returns early without setting `detailLoading[detailKey]`. When `entry.id` is absent (falsy), the row opens in expanded state, but no fetch is started and no loading/error UI is shown. `detailEntry` falls back to the summary `entry`, so all payload fields (headers, body) render as "(empty)". A user who expands such a row sees silently missing data with no indication of failure. The guard should be evaluated before `setExpandedId`, or an error state should be set when `entry.id` is missing.

`loadMore` appends `data.entries` to the current `entries` array (which may include SSE-injected entries) but advances `offset` by `limit` based on the previous API offset, not the current list length. If N entries arrived via SSE since the last fetch, the next `loadMore` call fetches at `offset + limit` — covering the same DB positions as some of the SSE-injected entries — and `setEntries` appends them without deduplication. The audit table can show duplicate rows for any entry that arrived both via SSE push and via the paginated API response.

`has_more` is declared optional (`has_more?: boolean`) in `AuditResponse` but is never read anywhere. `useAuditLog` computes `hasMore` independently as `entries.length < total`. The server-computed `has_more` (based on the actual entries returned from the same batch as `total`) is more reliable than the client-side recomputation, especially after SSE events adjust `entries` and `total` asymmetrically. Either consume `data.has_more` in the hook or remove the field from the interface to avoid the false impression that it is used.

`TestAuditList_OmitsPayloadsAndReturnsTotal` does not verify the `has_more` field under paginated conditions (e.g., inserting more entries than the requested limit). ardevd_jadx-collaboration_3-853179dc.message: The PR description promises a shared single-thread executor to serialize pull/push operations, but the actual code still uses `kotlin.concurrent.thread` for all four entry points. Each invocation spawns a fresh, unconstrained thread. Concurrent pulls and pushes remain fully possible on rapid key presses or menu clicks, leaving the interleaved repository read/write problem the PR claims to fix entirely unsolved.

`localRepository` is declared as `var localRepository: LocalRepository? = null` (nullable). Inside the non-inline `uiRun` lambda, it is passed directly to `localRepositoryToProject(localRepository: LocalRepository)` which requires a non-null type. Kotlin's smart-cast rules do not apply to captured `var` variables inside non-inline lambdas, so this is either a compile error under the K2 compiler or will throw a NullPointerException at runtime if the smart-cast is somehow accepted. The fix is to capture a non-nullable local copy before the lambda: `val repo = localRepository!!; uiRun { localRepositoryToProject(repo) }`.

`projectToLocalRepository` (and its callee `getProjectRenames`/`getProjectComments`) reads `context!!.args.codeData.renames` and `.comments` directly on the background thread. `localRepositoryToProject` (dispatched to the EDT via `uiRun`) writes those same fields via `setProjectRenames`/`setProjectComments`. Since multiple background threads can exist simultaneously (finding #1 — no serialization), concurrent reads on a background thread and writes on the EDT to these unsynchronized mutable fields constitute a data race.

`uiRun` delegates to `SwingUtilities.invokeLater` (asynchronous). Scheduling `localRepositoryToProject` inside `uiRun` means `pull()` returns — and the background thread exits — before the project state has actually been updated. If a new pull is triggered immediately afterwards (which is possible because no serialization exists), `projectToLocalRepository` in the new pull reads stale project renames/comments from before the previous pull's EDT update ran. The same problem applies to the equivalent block at the end of `push()` (lines 645–648).

`showError` (and `showInfo`) dispatch dialogs asynchronously via `invokeLater`. The background thread returns immediately after scheduling the error dialog, so a subsequent pull or push can start (and potentially show its own error) before the first dialog has even appeared on screen. This causes out-of-order dialogs and means the user may see an error for an operation they no longer regard as current. Previously, `JOptionPane.showMessageDialog` was blocking; the new async dispatch removes that back-pressure without any replacement synchronisation point.

In `push()`, `projectToLocalRepository(localRepository)` is called on the background thread at the top of the retry loop, reading `codeData.renames/comments`. However, the previous iteration's `writeRemoteRepository` and script have already updated the remote, and any pending `localRepositoryToProject` from a previous pull (dispatched asynchronously to the EDT) may not have run yet. This makes the `localRepository` snapshot built from project state inconsistent with what was last pushed to the remote, potentially re-introducing already-resolved renames into the next write.

`PluginMockery.pull` and `push` are still populated with the `{ kotlin.concurrent.thread { this.pull() } }` menu-action lambdas, but no test calls them any more — tests now invoke `plugin.pull()` / `plugin.push()` directly. Consequently, the tests never exercise the actual menu-triggered code path (which spawns a background thread), so any threading defect in that path, including the missing serialization, goes completely untested.

`kotlin.concurrent.thread` creates non-daemon threads by default, so a long-running script or blocked conflict dialog can keep the JVM alive after the UI is closed. The background worker should be daemonized or shut down explicitly to avoid shutdown stalls.

These shortcut handlers also create non-daemon threads via `kotlin.concurrent.thread`, so a blocked pull/push triggered from the keyboard can prevent JVM shutdown. Use a daemon executor thread or ensure the worker is shut down with the plugin lifecycle.

Any `EncryptedData` with `key_id = ""` (produced by the public `encrypt()` and `encrypt_with_aad()` functions, which both use `EncryptedData::new("", …)`) cannot be decrypted via a `with_keys()` layer — `key_for_id("")` returns `Err(StoreError::Backend)`. An operator who starts with `new()` mode, has records written by the pre-PR code or by callers of the public `encrypt` API, and then switches to `with_keys()` for key rotation will find those records permanently unreadable.

The public `encrypt()` function is still exported from `crates/credential/src/lib.rs` (line 118: `pub use crate::crypto::{EncryptedData, EncryptionKey, decrypt, encrypt}`) but now produces `EncryptedData` with `key_id = ""`. Any record written through this public API cannot be read back by an `EncryptionLayer::with_keys()` instance (which has no empty-string key alias). This silently creates data that is durable but unreadable once multi-key rotation is enabled, with no compile-time or runtime warning at write time.

`CredentialContext::resolve_credential` now passes `format!("{:?}", S::pattern())` — a non-unique category string like `"SecretToken"` — as the `expected_kind` argument to `CredentialResolverRef::resolve_scheme`. Previously this parameter carried `S::KIND`, a unique per-type string. Two different `AuthScheme` types that share the same `AuthPattern` (e.g., any two custom schemes both returning `AuthPattern::SecretToken`) will now receive the same string, silently breaking any resolver implementation that used the kind string for type-based dispatch. The `downcast::<S>()` call provides type safety, but if the resolver returns the wrong concrete type, the only error is `SchemeMismatch { actual: "unknown" }`, which gives no useful diagnostic.

`scheme_pattern` is stored as `format!("{:?}", S::pattern())`. Any two different `AuthScheme` types that both return `AuthPattern::Custom` (the escape hatch for plugin-defined patterns) will have identical `scheme_pattern` strings of `"Custom"`. When `project::<S>()` fails for such types the error reports `expected: "Custom", actual: "Custom"`, which is completely undiagnosable. Since `AuthPattern` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, adding new shared variants has the same problem. The type-safety of `downcast_ref` is unaffected, but error messages become useless.

The `TESTABLE: bool = false` const is now inconsistent with the new `test()` semantics. `test()` returns `Ok(None)` to signal non-testability, making the const redundant and misleading: a credential can return `Ok(Some(TestResult::Success))` from `test()` while still advertising `TESTABLE = false`, or vice versa. Caller code that gates `test()` invocations on `C::TESTABLE` (as suggested in the crate's plans, e.g. `plans/credential-flows-hld.md:542`) will skip testing for credentials that have correctly overridden `test()` but left `TESTABLE = false`.

The `decrypt` function returns a `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` to ensure the decrypted plaintext is zeroed on drop. However, the calling code in `EncryptionLayer` takes ownership of the inner `Vec<u8>` via `std::mem::take(&mut *plaintext)`, which circumvents the zeroizing behavior. The returned vector `credential.data` is a plain `Vec<u8>` and will not be zeroed when it goes out of scope, leaving sensitive data in memory. The `EncryptionLayer::get` method should return a zeroizing wrapper around the data.

Changing the built-in `CredentialState::KIND` values here makes existing stored credentials unreadable: `CredentialResolver::load_and_verify` rejects any record whose `state_kind` does not equal the new `C::State::KIND`, so previously stored API key records with `bearer` and basic-auth records with `basic_auth` will now fail resolution (and basic-auth also has a changed JSON field shape). This needs a compatibility path or explicit migration before the old kinds are removed.

This hard-coded value does not match `DEFAULT_MAX_PATHS`, which is still `10_000` above and is what `new()` assigns to `max_paths`. The docs now understate the cap by 10x and will drift if the constant changes; keep the intra-doc link or use the correct value.

NCATSTranslator_translator-ingests_336-e.message: `break` is used inside the `for record in data:` loop at lines 413, 530, 710, 925, and 1063 to indicate a record should be skipped ('not applicable'). `break` terminates the entire loop, so the first matching 'not applicable' record (e.g. Allosteric modulator/Neutral, Antagonist/Partial agonist, Fusion protein/Binding, None type/Binding or Competitive, Subunit-specific/Mixed) will silently stop processing all remaining records. Every occurrence must be replaced with `continue`.

Typo: `activator_list_with_separate_directly_physically_interacts_with_edge` contains `'Agnoist'` instead of `'Agonist'`. For `Type='Activator', Action='Agonist'` records, the list check fails so the record falls to the else branch (line 222), which does not handle 'Agonist'. The `ChemicalAffectsGeneAssociation` is still built but with `causal_mechanism_qualifier=None`. The inner `if record["Action"] == "Agonist"` at line 170 can never fire because 'Agonist' is not in the misspelled list.

Typo: `agnoist_list_with_separate_directly_physically_interacts_with_edge` contains `'Agnoist'` instead of `'Agonist'`. For `Type='Agonist', Action='Agonist'` records, `'Agonist' in ['Activation', 'Agnoist', ...]` evaluates to False, so neither the primary block nor any fallback block produces output. These records are silently dropped with no edge emitted. The inner `elif record["Action"] == "Agonist"` at line 263 is also unreachable for the same reason.

Typo: `allosteric_modulator_list_with_separate_directly_physically_interacts_with_edge` contains `'Agnoist'` instead of `'Agonist'`. For `Type='Allosteric modulator', Action='Agonist'` records, `'Agonist' in [... 'Agnoist' ...]` is False so the entire block is skipped and no edge is emitted. The inner `elif record["Action"] == "Agonist"` at line 341 is also unreachable.

pandas `groupby` drops rows where any key column contains NaN by default (`dropna=True`). `group_cols` includes `'Type'` and `'Action'`, both of which can be null in source data. Records with `Type=None` or `Action=None` are silently excluded from `source_agg_df` and never reach the transform. The transform code explicitly handles `record["Type"] is None` and `record["Action"] is None` cases, but they can never fire. Fix: pass `dropna=False` to `groupby`.

`predicate` is initialized as the string `"None"` instead of `None`. If any record type block omits setting `predicate` before building an association (e.g. Subunit-specific/Potentiation branch correctly sets it, but any unhandled action value in that same block would not), the invalid string `"None"` is passed as the predicate to `ChemicalAffectsGeneAssociation`. This is a regression from the original code where `predicate = None`.

`'Ligand Context'` is included in `sele_cols` but excluded from `group_cols`. The `drop_duplicates()` on `source_subset_df` uses `Ligand Context` to distinguish rows, causing rows that differ only in context to be kept as separate pre-aggregation entries. However, the subsequent `groupby` silently collapses them anyway (the column is dropped from the result). This means rows with different `Ligand Context` values but identical SPO+qualifier tuples will have their PubMed IDs merged without any record of the context distinction — the inclusion of `Ligand Context` in `sele_cols` serves no purpose and can mislead future readers about which columns drive deduplication.

In the `Inhibitor, Action not in list` branch, `causal_mechanism_qualifier` is only set when `Action == 'Feedback inhibition'`. For any other action value that is not in `inhibitor_list_with_separate_directly_physically_interacts_with_edge` and is not `'Feedback inhibition'`, `causal_mechanism_qualifier` is left as `None` (from the per-iteration reset at the top of the loop), and a `ChemicalAffectsGeneAssociation` is unconditionally constructed and appended. Unknown Inhibitor actions produce edges with no causal mechanism qualifier rather than being flagged or skipped.

For `Type='Allosteric modulator'`, `Action='Neutral'` and `Action=None` are both included in `allosteric_modulator_list_with_separate_directly_physically_interacts_with_edge` (line 331), so both enter the outer `if` block. The inner `elif` at line 411 then hits `break`, which (per finding #1) terminates the entire loop. Because `None` is explicitly in the list, any record in the real data with `Type='Allosteric modulator'` and a null Action value will kill the transform mid-stream regardless of the `break`→`continue` fix described separately.

Unnecessary check `if subject is not None and object is not None and association is not None` before appending to lists. The `subject` and `object` are always created, and if `association` were `None` due to a logic path not being taken, the code would not be inside this block. This check can be safely removed.

Hardcoded `str(uuid.uuid4())` is used for association IDs. The `entity_id()` utility function, which is used elsewhere in this file, should be used for consistency and to ensure a standardized ID generation scheme.

`print("not applicable")` writes to stdout from inside an ingest transform. Prefer using `koza.log(...)` (consistent with line 91 of the original code) so the message is captured by the framework's logging. The same pattern occurs at lines 529, 709, 924, and 1062.

The variable names `*_list_with_separate_directly_physically_interacts_with_edge` are extremely long (60+ characters) and are re-declared inside the per-record loop on each iteration. Consider moving these constants to module scope with shorter, descriptive names (e.g., `ACTIVATOR_ACTIONS_WITH_DPI_EDGE`) — this would also help readers see at a glance what categories exist and avoid repeated allocation per record.
Spelling: "seaparate" should be "separate". Same typo appears in the variable/comment naming throughout (e.g., the `agnoist_list_...` variable also misspells "agonist").

Trailing comma after `agent_type=AgentTypeEnum.manual_agent,` followed by a blank line before the closing `)` is harmless syntactically, but the stray blank line inside the constructor's argument list is inconsistent with all the other association constructors in this file. Consider removing the blank line on 999.

This changes emitted target nodes to `Protein`, but the ingest guide still documents UniProt target nodes under `node_category: biolink:Gene` in `src/translator_ingest/ingests/gtopdb/gtopdb_rig.yaml:178`. The RIG should be updated with the code change so the documented node output matches the actual graph.

This introduces a `biolink:related_to` edge, but `gtopdb_rig.yaml` documents only `affects`, `regulates`, and `directly_physically_interacts_with` for this ingest. Either the RIG needs a corresponding edge type or this branch should use a documented predicate; otherwise the emitted graph no longer matches the ingest specification.

mheuss_chronicle_14-04ac4c02.message: The function `walk_files_recursive` is designed to be a best-effort walk and swallows errors by logging a warning and returning. However, its public-facing caller `MediaManager::walk_files` does not propagate any error information, returning an empty `Vec`. This loss of information could mask filesystem issues, such as permission errors on subdirectories, from callers like `sweep_orphans` which might silently fail to scan parts of the media directory, leaving orphan files behind.

The error handling for `harden_file` attempts to clean up the newly created HEIF file on failure. However, if `storage.media_manager().delete_file()` also fails, the error from the deletion is logged but not propagated. The original error from `harden_file` is returned, but the file remains on disk with incorrect permissions, and the system is in a state where manual intervention may be required to fix both permissions and potential orphan files. This could be problematic if the permissions failure is persistent.

The startup orphan sweep logs errors but continues with daemon startup. If the sweep fails due to a transient issue, it's missed until the next restart. If it fails due to a persistent issue (e.g., directory permissions), it will fail on every startup, but the daemon will run anyway, potentially accumulating orphan files over time. Depending on the severity of the failure, a fatal exit might be more appropriate to alert an operator.

In `sweep_media_orphans`, if `media_mgr.delete_file` fails, the error is logged and the function continues. This could lead to a situation where `sweep_orphans` reports success (returning `Ok(bytes_freed)`) even if it failed to delete some or all of the orphan files it found, leaving them on disk.

After this refactor, the entire `files` module consists only of `#[cfg(test)]` helpers (`sanitize_id`, `date_parts`, `screenshot_path`, `audio_path`) and their tests. None of its functions are referenced from production code anymore, and the helpers reimplement the path/date logic that now lives in `media.rs` — so the tests verify a parallel implementation, not the real code path. Consider removing this module entirely (and the `pub(crate) mod files;` declaration in `lib.rs`) to avoid dead code drift, or convert these into tests of `MediaManager::allocate_path` that assert the expected `YYYY/MM/DD/<ts>_<id>.<ext>` layout against the actual production code.

`dummy_media_mgr()` uses a hard-coded shared path `/tmp/chronicle-test-dummy` that is created (but never cleaned up) and reused across every test that calls it. Because `cargo test` runs tests in parallel by default, several tests may concurrently share/own this directory, and on systems where `/tmp` is a symlink (e.g. macOS where `/tmp -> /private/tmp`) the canonicalization in `MediaManager::new` will resolve to a different path than the literal one passed in — which is fine here only because the dummy is never used for actual writes. Prefer creating a per-test `tempfile::tempdir()` (as `cleanup_handles_missing_files_gracefully` and the other tests already do) so each test gets an isolated, automatically-cleaned-up base directory.

`DirBuilder::mode` only affects directories created by this call. If the media/date directory already exists with more permissive permissions (for example from an older install or a previous run), this leaves it unchanged, so the storage hardening does not consistently enforce 0o700 on media directories.

This validation only constrains paths to the storage root, but `delete_file` is used on paths read from the database and `insert_screenshot`/`insert_audio_segment` accept caller-supplied paths. A malformed or legacy row pointing at another file under the root (for example `chronicle.db` or the IPC socket) would pass validation and be removable during cleanup; media operations should be constrained to the intended media subdirectories or validated at insert time.

`files` no longer has any non-test items or non-test references after moving file lifecycle logic into `media` (a repository search for `files::` returns no uses). Keeping it as a normal module leaves a dead production module just to host test-only helpers; consider removing it or moving those tests under `media` to avoid carrying obsolete structure.

This test helper uses a fixed `/tmp/chronicle-test-dummy` directory instead of a per-test temp directory, so tests can interfere across concurrent runs and leave persistent state on the developer/CI machine. Prefer returning a `TempDir` alongside the manager or constructing the manager from each test's existing temp root.

superhighfives_pika_200-b227aff0.message: swap() calls pushUndo() unconditionally before checking the active palette index. The PR description explicitly states named-palette swaps should not push to the undo stack, but the guard that would enforce this comes after the pushUndo() call. Every swap on a named palette corrupts the undo stack with auto-history snapshots.

deletePalette does not decrement activePaletteIndex when removing a palette whose index is less than the active one. Only the out-of-range case is clamped to 0. Deleting palette at index 1 while index 3 is active leaves activePaletteIndex pointing at the old palette 4 (now shifted to 3), silently switching the active tab to the wrong palette. The PR description says this decrement was implemented, but the code does not do it.

deletePalette does not call restoreAutoHistorySelection() after clamping activePaletteIndex to 0. When the active palette is deleted, activeHistoryID still holds the ID of the last selected pair from the deleted palette, which no longer exists in any palette. The selection state is stale until the user manually clicks a chip. The PR description says this was fixed.

applyEntry() calls recordHistory() whenever a pair from a named palette (activePaletteIndex != 0) is applied, including on every chip tap, context-menu apply, and palette navigation step. This means browsing or tapping chips in a named palette continuously writes entries to auto-history, and the undo stack grows with each chip selection. The behaviour is triggered both from navigatePrevious/navigateNext and from deleteCurrentEntry's fallback after deleting a chip.

deleteCurrentEntry: when the deleted chip was the last one in a named palette, the if-let guard on pairs.first is false and applyEntry is never called, so activeHistoryID still points to the just-deleted pair ID. The UI's selection indicator will be stale; subsequent navigatePrevious/navigateNext calls will find no active selection and fall back to the list boundary, which may be confusing.

migrateHistoryToPalettes() sets Defaults[.palettes] = [history], unconditionally replacing the entire palettes array with a single auto-history palette. If a partial migration occurred on a previous launch (palettes written, but colorHistory not yet cleared due to a crash), re-running migration would silently discard all named palettes the user had created. A safe migration should merge into palettes[0] if it already exists, not overwrite the array.

ISO8601DateFormatter() is constructed inside the pairs.map closure, creating one formatter instance per ColorPair rather than once per export call. ISO8601DateFormatter is expensive to initialise. The PR description states the formatter was hoisted out of the closure, but the code contradicts this — it is still allocated per iteration.

The compliance toggle button uses the same SF Symbol name for both on and off states: IconImage(name: showCompliance ? "checkmark.shield" : "checkmark.shield"). The conditional expression is identical in both branches, so the icon never changes when the feature is toggled. Only the foreground color changes (accent vs primary), providing minimal visual feedback.

ColorHistoryChip's context menu always labels the remove action as PikaText.textHistoryRemove ("Remove from history") regardless of whether the chip belongs to auto-history or a named palette. The PR description states the label switches between textHistoryRemove and textPaletteRemoveChip based on context, but ColorHistoryChip has no knowledge of which palette it belongs to and always uses the history string.

The export handler silently discards write errors with try?. If the file write fails (e.g., permissions, disk full), the user receives no feedback — the save panel closes and nothing happens. The PR description notes 'write errors s...' (truncated), suggesting this was identified but not fixed. At minimum the error should be surfaced via an alert.

The filename for exported palettes is generated by replacing spaces with hyphens, but it does not account for other characters that are invalid in filenames, such as `/` or `\`. This could cause the save operation to fail if the palette name contains such characters.
`import Defaults` is added here but `Exporter` and the new `paletteToJSON` method do not reference any `Defaults` APIs. This import can be removed.

After creating a palette, the new `current` pair is the only entry in the newly active palette, but `activeHistoryID` is left pointing at the previous history/palette entry. This means the just-created chip is not selected and keyboard delete/navigate starts from a stale selection until the user re-applies a chip.

`activePalette` falls back to `palettes.first` for an out-of-range index, but `isAutoHistory` is derived only from `activePaletteIndex == 0`. If the persisted index is out of range, the drawer displays auto-history entries while showing the named-palette add button and removal behavior, and there is no clamp elsewhere in the codebase.

For named palettes, the foreground/background apply actions still call the history-recording paths without restoring the palette chip selection. After applying one side of a named-palette chip, `activeHistoryID` points at the new auto-history entry rather than this palette chip, so the active highlight and keyboard delete/navigation in the palette become stale.

The existing `NotificationNamesTests` test every typed `Notification.Name` constant against its raw string. These new notification constants are not covered, so regressions in their raw values would bypass the suite. Add matching tests for the new names.

These new alert button titles are hard-coded, whereas the rest of the SwiftUI UI strings are routed through `PikaText`/`Localizable.strings` (for example `NavigationMenuItems.swift:130-153`). Add localized constants for these labels so the alert is translatable.

This notification is only observed by `PaletteTabBar`, which exists only while `ColorHistoryDrawer` is mounted. If the drawer is hidden (the default), choosing “New palette” from this menu posts to no active receiver, so nothing opens and no palette can be created from the menu.
`Defaults` is imported but not used anywhere in this file. Remove the unused import to keep dependencies clear and avoid lint/compiler warnings in stricter configurations.

gagneurlab_PROTRIDER_10-b462b109.message: NameError when training loss is non-finite: the branch assigns `auc_prec_rec = np.nan` but `return auprc` is executed unconditionally below it. If `~np.isfinite(loss)` is True, `auprc` is never defined in the local scope, so calling this with a diverged model raises NameError and crashes grid/binary search.

Binary search logic error: after the 'shrink the interval' block (when fM >= fL and fM >= fR) runs and updates L, fL, R, fR, control falls through to the bare `if fR > fM:` block instead of an `elif`. This causes the interval to be shifted in the same iteration it was already shrunk, producing incorrect search behaviour.

Loop variable `for q, fv in [(L,fL), (M,fM), (R,fR)]` shadows the outer `q` that holds the OHT-derived latent dimension used to seed L, M, R. After the inner for-loop, `q` equals `R` (the last tuple element). While `q = best_q` later restores the right value, any code between the loop and that assignment reads a corrupt `q`.

The checkpoint is always written after training because `checkpoint_path` is always a non-None Path object (either from config or defaulting to `out_dir/model.pt`). The PR claims checkpointing is now opt-in, but the code silently writes `out_dir/model.pt` on every run and reloads it on the next run, skipping retraining. This is a silent behaviour change for all users even when they have not set `checkpoint_path`.

`common_degrees_freedom` defaults to `True` in the Python dataclass but `config.yaml` explicitly sets it to `False`. Users invoking the Python API directly get the shared-df path; users running via config file get per-protein df. The two entry points produce different statistical results for the same data.

`gs_epochs: int = None` is incorrectly typed. The field defaults to `None` but is declared as `int`, violating the dataclass type annotation. It should be `Optional[int] = None`. Type checkers and runtime validation tools will flag this, and it is inconsistent with every other nullable field in the class.
Debug `print(data_shape)` left in `_get_gs_params`. This fires on every grid-search or binary-search run and cannot be suppressed by the `verbose` config flag, polluting all user output.

In the `use_common_df=False` branch of `_fit_t`, `df0` (the fallback for non-converged fits) is recomputed inside the sequential result loop from a partially-filled `df` array. Each non-converged protein is assigned a fallback derived only from previously processed proteins, so the fallback value changes unpredictably depending on processing order. This produces inconsistent per-protein df values compared to the intent described in the function's docstring.

`k_max = injected_dataset.X.shape[1]` is computed in the binary-search branch but never referenced afterwards. It appears to have been intended as an upper bound clamp for R (R = int(q * 3) can exceed the number of proteins), but the clamp was never applied. A latent dimension larger than the data dimension will cause model initialization to fail.

The PR description claims this is a small two-issue fix (removing an invalid `index=False` arg from `pd.read_parquet` and commenting out `checkpoint_path` in `config.yaml`). However, the actual diff is a large refactor: it removes cross-validation support entirely (deletes `cv.py`, `train_val`, `plot_cv_loss`, `tests/test_pipeline_cv.py`, and CV-related config fields), adds wandb integration, adds a binary-search `find_q_method`, introduces model save/load checkpointing, restructures `_fit_t` and `find_latent_dim`, changes `run()`'s return signature from a 2-tuple to a 4-tuple, switches activations from `ReLU` to `GELU`, etc. None of this is mentioned in the PR description. Either the PR description needs to be rewritten to accurately describe the scope of changes, or this PR should be split so the two small reviewer-flagged fixes are not bundled with an unrelated, much larger refactor.

For `method == "OHT"`, the branch body is just a log message — it relies on `q` computed unconditionally at lines 44-45. But for `method == "gs"`, lines 92-93 redundantly recompute `perform_svd()` and `find_enc_dim_optht()` (already done at lines 44-45). Additionally, for an integer `method` (e.g. `"5"`), the OHT computation at lines 44-45 is wasted work since `q` is overwritten at line 164. Consider moving the unconditional `perform_svd()` / `find_enc_dim_optht()` into the branches that actually need it (OHT and the `gs`/`bs` initial estimate).

`model_was_loaded` is computed as `(checkpoint_path and checkpoint_path.exists() and q is not None)`, but at this point in the code `q` is always set (either by `load_model` or by `find_latent_dim`), and `checkpoint_path.exists()` is also true if a previous run wrote a file even when loading just failed and a new untrained model was built at lines 485-491. In that failure case `should_train` becomes `False` and we run inference + statistics on a freshly initialized, untrained model. A more robust check is to track whether the load actually succeeded (e.g. set a flag right after the successful `load_model` call) instead of re-inferring it from path state and `q`.

These tests use hardcoded relative paths (`'sample_data/protrider_sample_dataset.tsv'`, `'sample_data/sample_annotations.tsv'`) that only resolve correctly when pytest is invoked from the repo root. The other test files in this directory consistently use the `protein_intensities_path` / `covariates_path` fixtures (see e.g. `tests/test_pipeline_standard.py`) which return absolute paths and are robust to the working directory. Please switch this file to the existing fixtures for consistency and to avoid flaky test discovery.

Test cases for cross-validation are deleted along with the CV code, but there is no replacement test coverage added for the substantial new functionality introduced in this PR: `load_model` error/failure paths, the binary-search (`bs`) `find_q_method`, the wandb integration code path, the `common_degrees_freedom=False` branch of `_fit_t`, and the early-stopping path in the new `train` function. Given the rest of the project has comprehensive pipeline tests, please add corresponding tests for at least the new public-facing options (`find_q_method='bs'`, `common_degrees_freedom=False`).

`fit_residuals` is exported as a public helper and previously accepted NumPy arrays, but it now unconditionally reads `res.columns`. Passing an array now raises `AttributeError`, which breaks existing callers unless the function either wraps arrays in a DataFrame or documents/restricts the input type.

The long-format save path no longer returns `df_res`, even though the docstring still says it returns the DataFrame and previous behavior did so. This silently breaks callers that use `summary = result.save(..., format='long')`; return `df_res` after writing it or update the API/documentation consistently.

Cross-validation support has been removed from the dispatcher instead of preserved behind `config.cross_val`; `cross_val` now fails config loading and the CV generators/tests were deleted. This is a breaking feature removal that is not part of the stated parquet/checkpoint fix and leaves existing users unable to run the documented k-fold/LOOCV workflow.

Although the validation above allows `mu`, `sigma`, and `df` to be scalars, these expressions unconditionally call `len()` on each value. Passing scalar distribution parameters now raises `TypeError`; branch on scalar types before indexing or calling `len`.

Grid-search results are now saved as `grid_search_results.csv` with columns `enc_dim`/`auprc`, but `plot_encoding_dim` still reads `grid_search.csv` and expects `encod_dim`/`aucpr`. After a `find_q_method='gs'` run, `protrider plot ... encoding_dim` will fail because the file and column names no longer match.

The new checkpoint format does not persist `h_dim`, but `load_model()` reconstructs the architecture from the current config. A checkpoint trained with `n_layers > 1` and a custom `h_dim` will fail to load, or load only when the caller happens to supply the same config value; architecture metadata needed for reconstruction should be saved with the checkpoint.

The return annotation says the fourth value is always `GridSearchResult`, but `gs_result` remains `None` when a checkpoint is loaded. Mark this as optional so API consumers and type checkers don't assume `to_csv()` is always available.

allan-mobley-jr_gimmes_468-e1477f8b.message: The `volume` field in StalenessEntry is written each cycle but never read back in the staleness logic. The new code only reads `entry["price"]`, `entry.get("open_interest", 0)`, and `entry["count"]` — `entry["volume"]` is never consulted. Storing it is misleading: the TypedDict requires it and it's persisted to disk each scan, but it has no effect on any decision.

`check_staleness` is called without the new `volume_floor` parameter, so it always falls back to the hardcoded default of 10. `volume_floor` is also absent from `ScannerConfig`, meaning users have no way to tune or override the threshold that is now the primary activity signal in the staleness filter.

`oi_changed = oi != entry.get("open_interest", 0)` defaults the missing field to 0. On first load of an old `scan_staleness.json` (without `open_interest`), every market with nonzero OI — essentially all real markets — will have `oi_changed=True`, resetting their accumulated stale count to 0. This silently voids all previously-built-up staleness state on migration, making the filter ineffective for another full `staleness_cycles` rounds.

`volume = m.volume_24h if m.volume_24h > 0 else m.volume` falls back to the lifetime cumulative `volume` field when `volume_24h` is zero. Any market with nonzero historical cumulative volume (even if completely inactive for months) will satisfy `has_volume >= volume_floor` and never be considered stale. This makes the fallback path counterproductive: it's intended to handle missing 24h data but actually permanently exempts high-history dead markets from staleness filtering.

scottlz0310_Mcp-Docker_29-e7705d26.message: PKCE is not enforced. ExchangeCode only verifies the code_challenge when sess.CodeChallenge != "", but the /authorize handler never requires code_challenge to be present. An attacker who obtains an internal authorization code (e.g. via referrer header, browser history, or log inspection) can call /token with no code_verifier and receive the GitHub access token. The Discovery endpoint advertises PKCE S256 as supported but the implementation makes it purely opt-in. PKCE should be required on every flow.

The /token endpoint performs no client_id validation. The comment claims GitHub validates client_id during code exchange, but that exchange happens at /callback, not at /token time. When /token is called, the internal code is already in the store and no outbound GitHub call is made. Combined with the missing PKCE enforcement, any party that obtains an internal code can present it to /token without supplying client_id and receive the GitHub access token. RFC 6749 §3.2.1 requires public clients to be identified at the token endpoint.

io.ReadAll(resp.Body) in ValidateToken has no size limit. A misbehaving reverse proxy or a response from a compromised network path could stream an unbounded body, exhausting process memory. SaveSession adds entries to the sessions map with no upper bound on the total count. Any unauthenticated caller can flood /authorize with distinct state values to fill the map indefinitely. The janitor only runs every minute, so a sustained burst can consume substantial memory between sweeps. There is no session count cap, no per-IP rate limit, and no rejection when the store is full.

The janitor goroutine started in NewStore runs forever with no stop mechanism. There is no context, done channel, or ticker.Stop() call. Every Store created (including in tests) leaks a goroutine for the lifetime of the process. This prevents orderly shutdown and causes goroutine leaks in any test that creates a Handler.

The redirect_uri allowlist check uses parsedRedirect.Hostname(), which strips the port. This means any port on an allowed host is accepted: both http://localhost:8080/callback and http://localhost:9999/evil pass the check when "localhost" is in AllowedRedirectHosts. An attacker running any service on localhost (or any allowed host) can receive the authorization code redirect. The check should include the port, or restrict to specific full origins.

The state query parameter is accepted with no length limit and stored verbatim as a map key in SaveSession. An attacker can submit a multi-megabyte state value in a single request, inflating the session map entry far beyond a normal key size. Combined with the lack of a session count cap, this makes the memory exhaustion DoS cheaper to execute per request.

Docker tooling that reads EXPOSE to discover the container's service port (e.g. `docker run -P`, some service mesh sidecars) will use 8083 regardless of the actual listening port. The Dockerfile should use a build arg or the EXPOSE should match the default in the entrypoint rather than a hardcoded literal.

In the `Callback` handler, the session is looked up via `lookupByCode` after the session is potentially modified by `CompleteCallback`. This re-lookup is unnecessary and potentially racy. `CompleteCallback` should return the `redirectURI` along with the `internalCode` so that the `Callback` function doesn't need to perform a second lookup.

Forwarding `err.Error()` from `ExchangeCode` directly into the `error_description` field leaks internal state to the client. In particular, the "session not found or expired for state %q" error from `session.go` will echo the client-supplied state value back in the response and the "redirect_uri mismatch" message can also be informative to attackers. Per RFC 6749 §5.2, `error_description` should be a human-readable explanation safe for the client, not an internal log message. Consider mapping internal errors to a generic message (e.g. "authorization code is invalid or expired") and keeping the detailed `err` only in the `slog.Warn` log line above.

When `ExchangeCode` fails due to `redirect_uri` mismatch or PKCE verification failure, the authorization code is left in `s.codes` and remains valid until TTL expiry. RFC 6749 §10.5 and RFC 7636 §4.6 require that an authorization code be invalidated as soon as it has been used (or attempted) so an attacker who obtains the code cannot brute-force the `code_verifier`. Recommend deleting the entry from `s.codes` (and the matching session) on any validation failure, not only on success.

The Discovery document advertises `code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"]`, but the `/authorize` and `/token` handlers treat PKCE as optional (no `code_challenge` parameter at `/authorize` results in `sess.CodeChallenge == ""`, and `ExchangeCode` then skips PKCE verification entirely). RFC 8414 / MCP clients (including Claude Desktop, per issue #28) will interpret the Discovery field as PKCE being mandatory. Either advertise that PKCE is optional, or enforce that `code_challenge` is required at `/authorize` (and `code_verifier` at `/token`) to match the advertised metadata.

`Callback` calls `CompleteCallback`, which leaves the original `s.sessions[state]` entry in place (it is only removed later when `/token` consumes the code). This allows the same `state` to be replayed against `/callback` — for example, if the redirect from GitHub is repeated by the browser — and each replay will issue a fresh internal code while overwriting `sess.InternalCode`, leaving orphan entries in `s.codes` that still reference the same underlying session. Consider invalidating the state on first successful callback (i.e. delete `s.sessions[state]` once an internal code has been issued) so a callback can be processed at most once.

No tests are included in `services/copilot-review-mcp/` for the OAuth façade, although issue #28's DoD and "テスト戦略" section explicitly require unit/E2E tests for Discovery, the OAuth flow, PKCE verifier mismatch, token validation, and session TTL. `ValidateToken` caches by raw GitHub access token used as a map key, and `extractBearer` does not enforce any minimum entropy or shape. A misbehaving (or malicious) client repeatedly sending different invalid tokens cannot poison the cache (`CacheToken` is only called after a successful GitHub `/user` response), but each unique invalid token causes a synchronous outbound call to GitHub with no rate limiting or negative caching. Consider adding a short negative cache (or single-flight) for tokens that GitHub has rejected with 401/403, to bound the request amplification an unauthenticated caller can produce against `api.github.com`.

The default `AllowedRedirectHosts` allowlist contains only `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`, and there is no configuration env var wired in `cmd/server/main.go` to extend it. This will reject any non-loopback MCP client `redirect_uri` (e.g. Claude Desktop installations using a custom scheme or a non-loopback host) with `invalid_request`, even though the issue/PR description targets such clients. Consider plumbing an env var (e.g. `ALLOWED_REDIRECT_HOSTS`) into `auth.Config.AllowedRedirectHosts` from `loadConfig`, or documenting that only loopback `redirect_uri`s are supported in phase 1.

PKCE is advertised in discovery but remains optional here: if a client omits `code_challenge`, the session is saved without one and `ExchangeCode` skips verifier validation. For this public OAuth façade, require `code_challenge` with S256 so intercepted internal authorization codes cannot be redeemed without a verifier.

`client_id` is not read or checked on the authorization request, so any caller can create a session that will later be exchanged as this façade's configured GitHub OAuth app. In a single-client façade, validate the incoming `client_id` against the configured client and store it with the session for the `/token` check.

When `COPILOT_REVIEW_MCP_PORT` is overridden, the container listens and publishes that port, but `BASE_URL` still defaults to `http://localhost:8083`. Discovery and GitHub callback URLs will point at the wrong port unless the user also remembers to set `BASE_URL`; derive the default from the same port variable or document/enforce the coupling.

The internal authorization code inherits the original session expiry from `/authorize`; `CompleteCallback` does not extend or set a code-specific expiry when the code is issued. If the user completes GitHub login near the session TTL, the redirect back to the client can carry a code that expires immediately and `/token` will reject it.

GitHub OAuth error callbacks (for example `?error=access_denied&state=...` when the user denies consent) are treated as a generic missing-code 400 and are not redirected back to the original client redirect URI. That leaves the MCP client without the OAuth error response it needs to finish the flow; look up the session by state and redirect with the error parameters when GitHub returns an OAuth error.
